study.title: Esther 6 - The unexpected reversal of Mardocyusund's honor
study.overview: This chapter shows a providential turn: just on the night that Haman planned the death of Mordecai, the king loses his sleep, consults the records of the kingdom and finds that Mordecai had never been rewarded for having denounced the conspiracy of the eunuchs. From there, the plot is reversed: Haman, who came to ask for the execution of Mordecai, ends up being the public instrument of his honor. The chapter ends with the humiliation of Haman and with the confirmation that his fall was already underway even before the banquet prepared by Esther.

outline.title: The king is led to remember the well forgotten
outline.explanation: That night, the king cannot sleep and sends to read the chronicles of the kingdom. There appears the record of the complaint made by Mordecai against the plot of Bigtã and Teres. The king asks what honor was given to Mordecai and finds that nothing has been done by him, which prepares the ground for late retribution.

outline.title: Haman plans his own humiliation
outline.explanation: As Haman arrives early in the courtyard to ask for Mordecai's death, the king calls him to answer a generic question about how to honor someone the king wants to distinguish. Haman, full of pride, imagines that the honor will be his and suggests real clothes, royal horse and public proclamation. But the king orders this just to Mordecai, and Haman must lead him through the city proclaiming his honor.

outline.title: Haman's fall advances as providence continues to act
outline.explanation: Mordecai returned to the post at the king's door, without displaying himself with the honor received, while Haman returns shot, with his head covered. In reporting everything to Zeres and friends, he receives from them the conclusion that Haman, Haman will not prevail against him. The conversation still doesn't end when the eunuchs arrive hurried to take Haman to the banquet prepared by Esther.

study.context: The notes mention that the ancient kings kept annals or chronicles of the reign, and it is from these records that the king remembers the service of Mordecai. It is also clear from the notes that the scenario is that of the Persian cut and that the public honor had great weight in that environment. The chapter fits between Haman's attempt to destroy Mordecai and Esther's intercession for his people.
study.theology: The main theological emphasis is the providence of God, which acts without being explicitly named in the text. The apparent chance is the king's insomnia, the right reading of the chronicles, the arrival of Haman at the exact moment - is presented by the commentators as God's sovereign direction to protect Esther, honor Mordecai and thwart Haman's perverse plan. The chapter also teaches moral reversal: the proud seeks exaltation for himself, but ends up serving the honor of the righteous; whoever prepares a trap can fall into it. Moreover, Mordecai's fidelity contrasts with the vanity of Haman. Mordecai does not turn honor into vanity, for it returns to its place; Haman, in turn, is consumed by shame. The response of Haman's friends in 13 shows that they see their situation as a sign of inevitable defeat, although the note does not fully explain the reason for this conclusion beyond Mardokaus' Jewish origin.

scholarViews.insight: The king's insomnia is not presented as mere coincidence, but as a means by which God works to protect Esther and Mordecai; the record of the chronicles leads to the memory of Mardoqueus' service.
The chapter shows God's providence by recommending Mordecai to the king's esteem just as Haman thinks that hanging will be consummated; the reversal prepares the defeat of the plan against the Jews.

The command to honor the man that the king desires to distinguish becomes, in practice, the humiliation of Haman and the exaltation of Mordecai; the divine providence exposes the vanity of human pride.

questions: What does the chapter teach about how God can act by seemingly common means, such as insomnia, official records and questions of the daily court?
In what ways did Haman's pride lead him to interpret the situation only in favor of himself?
How does Mordecai's attitude, which immediately returns to the king's door, contrasts with Haman's reaction to being humiliated?
study.practice: Watch carefully the small circumstances of the week, especially those that seem random or delayed, and ask God for discernment to recognize his direction in them. Also practice Mordecai's humility: receive honor without exalting and remaining faithful to his duty. Finally, examine if there are expectations of personal promotion similar to those of Haman in your heart, and replace them with obedient service, trusting that true honor belongs to God to grant it at the right time.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes do not explain why Zeres and the sages concluded that Haman would not prevail because of Martusan's Jewish origin. There is also no basis, in the given notes, to affirm additional historical details about date, specific geography or customs beyond what is mentioned about the actual records and the Persian court.
